title: Reading the News Well
objective: After this level you can judge whether a news story is reliable.
summary: Many shared links are never read. Journalists' own codes give readers clues: headlines backed by the text, clearly identified sources, labeled opinion, and prompt corrections.

cards.headline: In one study, most shared news links were never even clicked.
cards.body: In 2016, researchers at Columbia University and France's Inria found that 59% of the news links shared on Twitter in their sample were never clicked. Plenty of headlines travel without their stories. So how do you judge the story itself? Journalists' own rulebooks offer clues.

cards.headline: Clue 1: the headline isn't the story
cards.body: The UK's Editors' Code, enforced by the press regulator IPSO, tells the press not to publish misleading information, including headlines not supported by the text. That rule exists because the problem does. A headline is a pitch, written short. Read far enough to see whether the story actually backs it up.

cards.headline: Clue 2: who says so?
cards.body: The US Society of Professional Journalists' Code of Ethics tells reporters to identify sources clearly, so the public can judge how reliable they are and why they're talking. A trustworthy story shows its workings: named people, documents, data. If you can't tell how the reporter knows something, you can't check it either.

cards.headline: Clue 3: news or opinion?
cards.body: Both codes draw the same line. The SPJ says to label advocacy and commentary. The UK code says the press, while free to campaign, must distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact. Opinion isn't a flaw; it's a different product. Check the label before you treat an argument as a report.

cards.fact: A correction is a good sign, not a bad one.
cards.context: The SPJ tells journalists to correct mistakes promptly and prominently. The UK code says significant inaccuracies must be corrected promptly and with due prominence. An outlet that runs corrections is showing you it checks its own work.

cards.headline: The news: read well
learned: 59% of shared links in one study went unclicked
Headlines must be backed by the story
Opinion is labeled; mistakes get corrected

questions.prompt: In the 2016 Columbia and Inria study, what share of the shared news links in the sample were never clicked?
questions.explanation: The researchers found 59% of the news links shared on Twitter in their sample were never clicked.

questions.prompt: Why is a published correction a good sign about a news outlet, according to journalists' codes?

options.label: It proves the outlet has never made a mistake
options.rationale: A correction means it did, and fixed it.

options.label: The codes ask outlets to fix mistakes promptly and prominently
It means the story was only opinion
options.rationale: Corrections fix errors of fact in any story.

questions.explanation: Both the SPJ code and the UK Editors' Code expect mistakes to be corrected promptly and prominently, so corrections show an outlet checking itself.

questions.prompt: Level 69's SIFT says to investigate the source and trace claims. Which rule in the journalists' codes makes that easier?

options.label: Correct mistakes promptly
options.rationale: Corrections help, but don't show where a claim came from.

options.label: Keep headlines short and punchy
options.rationale: The codes ask headlines to match the story, not to be short.

options.label: Publish opinion without a label
options.rationale: The codes say to label opinion.

questions.explanation: The SPJ code tells reporters to identify sources clearly, which is exactly what you need to investigate a source and trace a claim.
